notes: Two phrasal expressions are slightly above a true beginner but do not block meaning in context: 'Hercules took hold of him.' could be 'Hercules caught him.'; 'But Hercules held on.' could be 'But Hercules did not let go.' or 'But Hercules held him tight.'
'At last the old man stopped.' is a little vague (stopped what?); 'At last the old man stopped changing.' or 'At last the old man was a man again.' is clearer.
'Then the sky is not so heavy.' is acceptable at A1; 'Then the sky will not be so heavy' is more natural but uses future, so leaving it is fine.

Tenses are present/past simple plus modal 'can'; no conditionals, relatives, passives or perfects. Vocabulary (deer, snake, power, shoulders) is basic; only a couple of words would need help, well under the limit.
'Hercules thought fast.' is fine; 'Hercules thought quickly.' is marginally more standard.
Sequence and quiz keys are consistent with A1 and with the higher levels.
No conditionals or passive found; 'only on one condition' is lexical, not a conditional structure.
Relative clauses ('who was stronger than anyone', 'whose name was Antaeus') are within B1 range.
Quiz items are unambiguous with correct keys.
'wildly' appears twice in consecutive sentences ('a deer, kicking wildly' / 'a seabird that beat its wings wildly'); consider 'beat its wings furiously' for the second.
'The giant said, ...' directly after '...the giant stopped a little way off' repeats 'the giant'; 'He said' or 'Atlas said' reads more smoothly.

'"Who are you, little man, and what brings you to the end of the world?" called Atlas, for that was who it was, from somewhere up among the clouds.' The embedded clause is a deliberate literary reveal but slightly clumsy; could be '...called a voice from somewhere up among the clouds, for the giant was Atlas.'
Prose is genuinely literary (inversion 'Hardly had Hercules adjusted his hold when...', 'stronger than he was clever') rather than padded.
Fight and shape-changing are gentle (snapping, growling, coiling) and stay within 4+ guidelines.

summary: A faithful, child-friendly retelling of Hawthorne's 'The Three Golden Apples': the flower-weaving maidens, the shape-changing Old Man of the Sea, Antaeus lifted off the earth, the golden cup crossing, and Atlas tricked into taking back the sky with the lion-skin cushion ruse, in the right order and with the right ending. All five levels meet their grammar constraints, are internally consistent, contain no age-inappropriate content, and have correctly keyed quizzes; only minor stylistic notes remain.
